states.name: Execution Architecture
states.description: Watcher execution is driven by the SchedulerService (scheduler_service.rs). The service checks for due watcher tasks in its tick() loop, then calls execute_watcher(watcher_id). The execution flow: (1) load watcher definition from PgDb::get_watcher(), (2) check enabled flag (skip if disabled), (3) run PgDb::search_timeline_filtered() with the watcher's timelineQuery and optional app/source filters, fetching up to 200 results, (4) parse the lookbackWindow via parse_lookback_window() which converts strings like '15 minutes' into a chrono::DateTime cutoff and post-filter results by created_at, taking at most 50, (5) format the reasoning_prompt template by replacing {{results}} with a numbered list of timeline entries, {{result_count}} with the count, and {{query}} with the original query, (6) send the formatted prompt to the runner's own /prompts/run HTTP API via reqwest, (7) record the execution result via PgDb::record_watcher_run() which sets last_run_at=NOW() and stores the AI response text in last_result_json. The SchedulerService receives pg_db: Option<Arc<PgDb>> from main.rs via start_scheduler_service(). The Watcher step type in step_types.rs has a 120-second expected duration. The ScheduledTaskType::Watcher variant in scheduler.rs carries the watcher_id.

states.name: Data Model and Storage
states.description: Watchers are stored in the PostgreSQL 'watchers' table with columns: id (TEXT PK, UUID generated on create), name, schedule_json (ScheduleExpression as JSON), timeline_query (FTS query string), app_name_filter (nullable), source_type_filter (nullable), lookback_window (TEXT, default '15 minutes'), reasoning_prompt (TEXT with {{results}}/{{result_count}}/{{query}} placeholders), action_json (WatcherAction as JSON), enabled (BOOLEAN, default true), last_run_at (nullable TIMESTAMPTZ), last_result_json (nullable TEXT), created_at, updated_at. The table is created via ensure_tables() on PgDb startup. Queries are generated by Clorinde from queries/watchers.sql with nullable annotations (last_run_at?, last_result_json?, app_name_filter?, source_type_filter?) ensuring proper Option<T> types in Rust. The PgDb wrapper (database/pg/watchers.rs) uses a map_watcher_row! macro to convert Clorinde row types to the app-level Watcher struct. CRUD operations are exposed as 6 Tauri commands registered in main.rs.

states.name: Implementation Details
states.description: Frontend: WatcherManagementPanel (React, components/activity-timeline/WatcherManagementPanel.tsx) uses useState for watchers list, showForm toggle, form data, editingId, and loading state. useEffect calls loadWatchers() on mount via list_watchers Tauri command. Form defaults: name='', timelineQuery='', scheduleInterval='5 minutes', lookbackWindow='15 minutes', actionType='LogOnly', reasoningPrompt=default template with placeholders. Create calls create_watcher with JSON-serialized schedule ({type:'interval',value:scheduleInterval}) and action ({type:actionType}). Toggle calls set_watcher_enabled with inverted boolean. Delete calls delete_watcher. All mutations call loadWatchers() after completion. The component is lazy-loaded in TabContent.tsx. Tab ID 'watchers' registered in tab-types.ts. Sidebar item in qontinui-navigation/src/groups.ts under OBSERVE_ITEMS with Eye icon and #06B6D4 cyan color, runner-only platform. Watcher cards rendered with border-border, hover:bg-accent/50. Enabled toggle uses ToggleRight (text-green-500), disabled uses ToggleLeft (default muted). Delete button uses hover:text-destructive. Query displayed in code element with bg-muted.

states.name: Relationship to Activity Timeline
states.description: Watchers depend entirely on the activity timeline for their data source. A watcher's timeline_query is executed against the same activity_timeline PostgreSQL table that the Activity Timeline page searches. The three capture sources that feed the timeline (BackgroundObserver, Python bridge, BackgroundCaptureService) indirectly feed watchers. The lookback_window determines how far back a watcher searches, preventing it from reasoning over stale data. Watchers and the Activity Timeline share the same Observe sidebar group and are positioned adjacent to each other in the navigation.

description: The Watchers page lets users create, manage, and monitor scheduled AI agents that watch the activity timeline for specific patterns. Each watcher runs on a schedule, queries the timeline using full-text search, feeds the results into an AI reasoning prompt, and optionally triggers an action. The page loads the watcher list on mount via the list_watchers Tauri command and provides inline creation, enable/disable toggling, and deletion. Watchers are stored in a PostgreSQL table and executed by the runner's scheduler service.
